title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
content:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

title: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
content:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

title: The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)
content:
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes, analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

title: The Directing Genius of Akira Kurosawa Explained
content: Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa, but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, Throne of Blood, The Bad Sleep Well, and Ran were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from The Magnificent Seven and A Fistful of Dollars in the nineteen-sixties to Living and Highest 2 Lowest in this decade.

title: When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)
content: “La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

title: Watch Accurate Recreations of Medieval Italian Longsword Fighting Techniques, All Based on a Manuscript from 1404
content:
Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: this writer did not attend). The gathering of the Joshes in April 2021 in Nebraska could not have been more peaceful, including its finishing battle royale, conducted with pool noodles.

The Joshes had no concern for proper pool-noodle-wielding technique, if there is such a thing. But groups of people who gather around the country to stage medieval-style battles in live-action role playing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might benefit from pointers.

So, too, might those who choreograph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can serious historical re-creators learn how to wield a real blade in historically accurate combat? One resource can be found at Wiktenauer, a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

title: Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
content:
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch, Girl with a Pearl Earring, and The Garden of Earthly Delights. But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece, also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece, seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

title: How Isaac Newton Lost $3 Million Dollars in the “South Sea Bubble” of 1720: Even Geniuses Can’t Prevail Against the Machinations of the Markets
content:
The Aristotelian notion of “man” as a “rational animal” has seen its share of detractors, from the Cynics to Bertrand Russell to nearly the whole of Poststructuralist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to compress the debate between intellect and passion into a pithy aphorism: “Man is a rational animal who always loses his temper when he is called upon to act in accordance with the dictates of reason.”

We no longer need clever verbal barbs to refute too-optimistic assessments of human behavior. Economics is catching up: we have the language of neuroscience and psychology, which consistently tells us that humans decidedly do not behave rationally very often, but are driven by bias and biology in inexplicable ways. And for over a hundred years now, we’ve known that the clockwork Newtonian view of the physical universe turns out to be a much messier and indeterminate affair, as does the universe of the human mind.

title: Behold the Gloriously Cheap 1970s Italian Knockoffs Inspired by Star Wars
content:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above. “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars, or even a Navajo Joe. Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

title: How Leo Tolstoy Became a Vegetarian and Jumpstarted the Vegetarian & Humanitarian Movements in the 19th Century
content:
Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker, “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
content: Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

title: European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche: A Free Online Course from Yale
content:
Taught by historian Marci Shore, “European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche” surveys the story of modern thought, from the late 18th century to the late 20th.

Along the way, the course explores major trends in modern European thought: Marxism-Leninism, psychoanalysis, expressionism, structuralism, phenomenology, existentialism, anti-politics, and deconstruction. Intellectual figures covered in the course include Nietzsche, Lenin, Kafka, Freud, Husserl, de Beauvoir, Heidegger, Arendt, Adorno, Sartre, Girard, Foucault, Derrida, and Havel.

You can watch all 25 lectures above. Or find them on YouTube and Apple Podcasts. Explore the course handouts here.

“European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche” will be added to our collection, 1,700 Free Online Courses from Top Universities.

title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
content:
Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twitter

The prolific Hans Zimmer scored Christopher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Batman Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson. Just what difference this has made in the resulting pictures is a matter best left to the scrutiny of the most obsessive fans, but any viewer can hear how much Zimmer and Göransson differ stylistically. This past summer, the siren song included on the soundtrack of The Odyssey featured one of the latter’s particularly notable choices: the use of an aulos, a double-reeded wind instrument much played back in ancient Greece.

Though Göransson didn’t have a genuinely ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound produced by the replica proved evocative enough. But just this year, as it happens, a bone flute actually dating from the period in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archaeological site of ancient Troy in modern-day northwestern Turkey.

title: When Salvador Dali Met Sigmund Freud, and Changed Freud’s Mind About Surrealism (1938)
content:
The close associations between Surrealism and Freudian psychoanalysis were liberally encouraged by the most famous proponent of the movement, Salvador Dalí, who considered himself a devoted follower of Freud. We don’t have to wonder what the founder of psychoanalysis would have thought of his self-appointed protégé.

We have them recording, in their own words, their impressions of their one and only meeting—which took place in July of 1938, at Freud’s home in London. Freud was 82, Dalí 34. We also have sketches Dalí made of Freud while the two sat together. Their memories of events, shall we say, differ considerably, or at least they seemed totally bewildered by each other. (Freud pronounced Dalí a “fanatic.”)

In any case, there’s absolutely no way the encounter could have lived up to Dalí’s expectations, as the Freud Museum London notes:

[Dalí] had already travelled to Vienna several times but failed to make an introduction. Instead, he wrote in his autobiography, he spent his time having “long and exhaustive imaginary conversations” with his hero, at one point fantasizing that he “came home with me and stayed all night clinging to the curtains of my room in the Hotel Sacher.”
